<B><U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">PART I</FONT></U></B></DIV>
  <DIV

<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Item 1.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;&#160; </FONT>Business</FONT></B></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">General</FONT></B></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<I><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></I></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Bank of Kentucky Financial Corporation (&#8220;BKFC&#8221;) is a bank holding company that was incorporated as a Kentucky corporation in 1993 and engaged in no business activities until 1995, when BKFC acquired all of the issued and outstanding shares of common stock of The Bank of Kentucky, Inc. (the &#8220;Bank&#8221;), a bank incorporated under the laws of the Commonwealth of Kentucky (formerly named The Bank of Boone County, Inc.), and Burnett Federal Savings Bank (&#8220;Burnett&#8221;), a federal savings bank that was later merged into the Bank.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>BKFC, through the Bank, is engaged in the banking business in northern Kentucky and Hamilton county, Ohio.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Formed in 1990, the Bank provides financial services and other financial solutions through 32 offices located in northern Kentucky, which includes Boone, Kenton and Campbell counties and parts of Grant, Pendleton and Gallatin counties in northern Kentucky, and Hamilton county in Ohio.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The principal products produced and services rendered by the Bank are as follows:</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <TABLE
style="MARGIN-TOP: 0pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman; MARGIN-BOTTOM: 0pt; TABLE-LAYOUT: fixed; CLEAR: both; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; dtth: tableHanging" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" width="100%">
    <TR
style="PADDING-BOTTOM: 0pt; VERTICAL-ALIGN: top; PADDING-TOP: 0in">
  <TD
style="WIDTH: 0.75in; WORD-WRAP: break-word; VERTICAL-ALIGN: top">
</TD>
  <TD
style="WIDTH: 0.25in; WORD-WRAP: break-word; VERTICAL-ALIGN: top">
<FONT style="FONT-FAMILY: Symbol; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#183;</FONT></FONT></TD>
  <TD
style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; WORD-WRAP: break-word; VERTICAL-ALIGN: top">
<U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Commercial Banking</FONT></U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"> &#150; The Bank provides a full range of commercial banking services to corporations and other business clients.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Loans are provided for a variety of general corporate purposes, including financing for commercial and industrial projects, income producing commercial real estate, owner-occupied real estate and construction and land development.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank also provides a wide range of deposit services, including checking, lockbox services and other treasury management services.</FONT></TD>
</TR>
</TABLE>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt 0.75in; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <TABLE

    <TR

  <TD

</TD>
  <TD

<FONT style="FONT-FAMILY: Symbol; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#183;</FONT></FONT></TD>
  <TD
style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; WORD-WRAP: break-word; VERTICAL-ALIGN: top">
<U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Consumer Banking</FONT></U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"> &#150; The Bank provides banking services to consumers, including checking, savings and money market accounts as well as certificates of deposits and individual retirement accounts.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank also provides consumers with electronic banking products like internet banking, debit cards and 56 ATMs.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In addition, the Bank provides consumer clients with installment and real estate loans and home equity lines of credit.</FONT></TD>
</TR>

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <TABLE

    <TR

  <TD

<U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Trust Services</FONT></U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"> &#150; The Bank offers specialized services and expertise in the areas of fiduciary services and wealth management.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The fiduciary services include administration of personal trusts and estates.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Wealth management services include investment management of accounts for individuals, institutions and not-for-profit entities.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Also, brokerage and insurance products are offered through the Bank&#8217;s broker-dealer relationship with Cetera, Inc.</FONT></TD>

  <DIV

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The majority of the Bank&#8217;s loan portfolio, approximately 77%, consists of loans secured with or by real estate.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Loans secured with real estate are further broken down by loan type and borrower.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Included in loans secured with or by real estate as of December 31, 2013 are:</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: -0.25in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt 1in; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <TABLE
style="MARGIN-TOP: 0pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman; MARGIN-BOTTOM: 0pt; TABLE-LAYOUT: fixed; CLEAR: both; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; dtth: tableHanging" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" width="100%">

</TD>

<FONT style="FONT-FAMILY: Symbol; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#183;</FONT></FONT></TD>
  <TD
style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; WORD-WRAP: break-word; VERTICAL-ALIGN: top">
<U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Residential real estate loans</FONT></U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"> - $283 million or 23% of loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;&#160; </FONT>These loans are secured by residential properties, where the repayment comes from the borrower&#8217;s personal cash flows and liquidity, and collateral values are a function of residential real estate values in the markets we serve.</FONT></TD>
</TR>
</TABLE>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt 0.75in; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <TABLE

    <TR

  <TD

</TD>
  <TD

<FONT style="FONT-FAMILY: Symbol; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#183;</FONT></FONT></TD>
  <TD
style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; WORD-WRAP: break-word; VERTICAL-ALIGN: top">
<U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Commercial real estate loans</FONT></U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"> - $372 million or 30% of loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>This loan type includes non-owner-occupied commercial real estate loans and construction and land development loans. These loans are made to borrowers where the primary source of repayment is derived from the cash flows generated by the real estate collateral.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>These loans are secured by property such as apartment complexes, retail centers and land which is being developed and sold.</FONT></TD>
</TR>
</TABLE>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <TABLE
style="MARGIN-TOP: 0pt; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman; MARGIN-BOTTOM: 0pt; TABLE-LAYOUT: fixed; CLEAR: both; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; dtth: tableHanging" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" width="100%">

<FONT style="FONT-FAMILY: Symbol; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#183;</FONT></FONT></TD>
  <TD
style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; WORD-WRAP: break-word; VERTICAL-ALIGN: top">
<U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Owner-occupied commercial real estate loans</FONT></U><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"> - $302 million or 24% of loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>These are loans secured by real estate where the operating business is the source of repayment.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>These properties serving as collateral are characterized as industrial, warehouse or office.</FONT></TD>

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">BKFC&#8217;s senior management monitors and evaluates financial performance on a company-wide basis.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>All of BKFC&#8217;s financial service operations are similar, and considered by management to be aggregated into one reportable operating segment for purposes of generally accepted accounting principles, although certain management responsibilities are assigned by business line.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Accordingly, all of BKFC&#8217;s operations are aggregated in one reportable operating segment in this Annual Report on Form 10-K (this &#8220;Annual Report&#8221;).<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Revenue, net income and total assets for the years ended December 31, 2013, 2012 and 2011 are presented below:</FONT></DIV>

  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">As described in more detail in this Annual Report, the recent economic recession and ongoing economic recovery have had a substantial effect on the operations of BKFC and the Bank.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In an effort to stabilize and strengthen the financial markets and the banking industry, the United States Congress and various federal agencies have taken a number of significant actions over the past several years, including the passage of legislation and the implementation of a number of programs.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The most recent of these actions was the passage into law, on July 21, 2010, of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (the &#8220;Dodd-Frank Act&#8221;).<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>See below under &#8220;Regulation and Supervision&#8221; for further discussion of the Dodd-Frank Act.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">BKFC and the Bank participated in two government programs enacted in response to the recession.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>First, in October 2008 the Bank participated in the transaction account guarantee component of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation&#8217;s (the &#8220;FDIC&#8221;) Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program (the &#8220;TLGP&#8221;), whereby the FDIC would temporarily guarantee all depositor funds in qualifying non-interest-bearing transaction accounts.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Second, in February 2009 BKFC participated in the Capital Purchase Program (&#8220;CPP&#8221;) as part of the Troubled Asset Relief Program (&#8220;TARP&#8221;) sponsored by the United States Department of the Treasury (the &#8220;Treasury Department&#8221;), in order to enhance BKFC&#8217;s liquidity and capital position.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>BKFC received $34.0 million under the CPP in exchange for issuing 34,000 shares of Fixed Rate Cumulative Perpetual Preferred Stock, Series A (the &#8220;Series A Preferred Stock&#8221;), and a warrant (the &#8220;Warrant&#8221;) to purchase approximately 274,784 shares of BKFC common stock (&#8220;Common Stock&#8221;).<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Treasury Department&#8217;s authority to make new investments under the CPP expired in October 2010.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>On December 22, 2010, BKFC effected the repurchase of one-half of the outstanding $34 million of Series A Preferred Stock held by the Treasury Department.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>On November 23, 2011, BKFC effected the repurchase of the final $17 million of Series A Preferred Stock held by the Treasury Department.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In the second quarter of 2013, the Company completed the repurchase of the Warrant for an aggregate repurchase price of $2,150,649. Prior to the repurchase transaction, the Warrant permitted the Treasury Department to purchase 276,078.12 shares of the Company&#8217;s common stock at an exercise price of $18.473 per share. Neither BKFC nor the Bank has actively participated in any of the other wide-ranging programs that were instituted by the federal government in response to the economic recession.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>For a discussion of the impact of the current economic conditions on the financial condition and results of operations of BKFC and its subsidiaries, see below under &#8220;The Current Economic Environment,&#8221; as well as &#8220;Item 7. Management&#8217;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations&#8221; in this Annual Report.</FONT></DIV>

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">As a bank incorporated under the laws of the Commonwealth of Kentucky, the Bank is subject to regulation, supervision and examination by the Department of Financial Institutions of the Commonwealth of Kentucky (the &#8220;Department&#8221;) and the FDIC.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank is also a member of the Federal Home Loan Bank of Cincinnati (the &#8220;FHLB&#8221;).</FONT></DIV>

  <DIV

  <DIV

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">On June 14, 2000, BKFC consummated the acquisition of the Fort Thomas Financial Corporation (&#8220;FTFC&#8221;) and its wholly owned subsidiary, the Fort Thomas Savings Bank (&#8220;FTSB&#8221;).<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>FTFC was merged with and into BKFC and FTSB was merged with and into the Bank.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Upon consummation of this acquisition, 865,592 shares of Common Stock were issued for substantially all of the outstanding shares of FTFC.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The combination was accounted for as a pooling of interests and the historical financial position and results of operations of the two companies have been combined for financial reporting purposes.</FONT></DIV>

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">On November 22, 2002, BKFC consummated the acquisition of certain assets and assumption of certain liabilities of Peoples Bank of Northern Kentucky (&#8220;PBNK&#8221;).<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>This acquisition was accounted for under the purchase method of accounting and, accordingly, the tangible and identifiable intangible assets and liabilities of the purchase were recorded at estimated fair values.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The excess of the purchase price over the net tangible and identifiable intangible assets was recorded as goodwill.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The adjustments necessary to record tangible and identifiable intangible assets and liabilities at fair value are amortized to income and expensed over the estimated remaining lives of the related assets and liabilities.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">

  <DIV

<FONT style="LETTER-SPACING: -0.1pt; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">On May 18, 2007, </FONT><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">BKFC consummated the acquisition of<FONT style="LETTER-SPACING: -0.1pt"> FNB Bancorporation, Inc. and its subsidiary, First Bank of Northern Kentucky, Inc. (&#8220;First Bank&#8221;).<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT>This acquisition was accounted for under the purchase method of accounting and, accordingly, the tangible and identifiable intangible assets and liabilities of the purchase were recorded at estimated fair values.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The excess of the purchase price over the net tangible and identifiable intangible assets was recorded as goodwill.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The adjustments necessary to record tangible and identifiable intangible assets and liabilities at fair value are amortized to income and expensed over the estimated remaining lives of the related assets and liabilities.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">On December 11, 2009, the Bank completed the purchase of three banking offices of Integra Bank Corporation&#8217;s wholly-owned bank subsidiary, Integra Bank N.A. (&#8220;Integra Bank&#8221;), located in Crittenden, Dry Ridge and Warsaw, Kentucky and a portfolio of selected commercial loans originated by Integra Bank&#8217;s Covington, Kentucky loan production office.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>This transaction also included the deposits of two additional branches in northern Kentucky where the banking offices were excluded.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>This transaction added $76 million in deposits and $51 million in loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The deposits were purchased at a premium of 6.50%, while the loans were purchased at an approximate 1% discount.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The acquisition included a core deposit intangible asset of $1.579 million and goodwill of $5.31 million.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In a separate transaction, the Bank also bought an additional $49 million in loans from Integra Bank in the third quarter and $7 million in the fourth quarter of 2009 at an approximate 1% discount.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;&#160; </FONT>None of these purchased loans had shown evidence of credit deterioration since origination</FONT></DIV>

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">On December 31, 2009, the Bank completed the purchase of Tapke Asset Management, LLC (&#8220;TAM&#8221;). TAM was an independent investment advisory firm, headquartered in Fort Wright, Kentucky, and one of northern Kentucky&#8217;s largest independent investment advisory firms.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>As a result of this transaction, the Bank&#8217;s client assets increased to over $650 million at December 31, 2009.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>TAM was purchased for $3 million, consisting of $2 million in cash and $1 million in Common Stock, with an additional $500,000 in contingent consideration payable in three years based on revenue retention, which had a fair value of $395,000 and was paid out in 2012.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The acquisition included a customer relationship intangible of $1,525,000, a non-compete agreement intangible of $320,000, a trade name intangible of $165,000 and goodwill of $1,370,000.</FONT></DIV>

style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">On October 28, 2011, the Bank completed the purchase of one banking office of the United Kentucky Bank of Pendleton County, Inc. (&#8220;United Kentucky Bank&#8221;), located in Falmouth, Kentucky and a portfolio of selected loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>This acquisition was consistent with the Bank&#8217;s strategy to strengthen and expand its northern Kentucky market share.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>This transaction added $28 million in deposits and $14 million in loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The deposits were purchased at a $300,000 premium, while the loans were purchased at an approximate 1.58% discount.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The acquisition included a core deposit intangible asset of $511,000 and goodwill of $134,000.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The results of operations for this acquisition have been included since the transaction date of October 28, 2011.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Current Economic Environment </FONT></B></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 24.5pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">During 2013, the nation continued to experience a slow economic recovery. While the recovery remains fragile and is still threatened by slow jobs growth, the economic outlook in the markets in which we operate continue to show signs of weaker asset quality levels in the residential and commercial mortgage markets, household and business uncertainty as well as tight credit conditions.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank anticipates that the effects of the financial crisis and recession are expected to continue for the near future, especially as the magnitude of economic distress facing local markets places continued pressure on asset quality and earnings, with the potential for undermining the stability of the banking organizations that serve these markets.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 24.5pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Although the Bank has experienced an increase in defaults and foreclosures during the last five years, such levels have been significantly less than other regions of the United States. This is due, in part, to the fact that the Bank&#8217;s markets in northern Kentucky and Cincinnati, Ohio have not experienced as dramatic a reduction in real estate values from previous years compared with markets like Florida and California.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>

  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;BACKGROUND-COLOR: rgb(0,0,0); FONT-STYLE: normal; PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always; TEXT-INDENT: 0in; MARGIN: 0in; HEIGHT: 1px; CLEAR: both; FONT-SIZE: 1px" contenteditable="false">
</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 24.5pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">As a result of management concerns over the current economic environment, individual lending authorities remain at reduced levels and the loan committee structure established in 2009 remains in place, which added the Bank&#8217;s Chief Executive Officer to the Bank&#8217;s loan committee to further scrutinize credit decisions. Additionally, the Bank previously established a problem asset workout group in 2009. This group&#8217;s primary task is to reduce risk by accelerating the exit from troubled credits. The problem asset workout group does this employing a number of strategies.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In addition, this group provides advice and support for the Bank&#8217;s lending professionals with respect to those relationships that are showing signs of stress but have not elevated to the point of transfer to workout.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In addition to these monitoring and management processes, BKFC also conducts quarterly reviews and evaluations of all criticized loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>These comprehensive reviews, which pre-date the recent economic recession, include the formulation of action plans and updates on recent developments on all criticized loans. Proactive management of problem loans remains a high priority of the Bank&#8217;s senior management. </FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 24.5pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">BKFC has not experienced the stress or deterioration in its residential real estate portfolio that other financial institutions may be experiencing, as residential real estate loans represent a small portion of the Bank&#8217;s overall loan portfolio. The Bank has not created or marketed any sub-prime loan products to its customers and does not service mortgages on behalf of other institutions. The Bank follows a strategy of selling a majority of its originated residential loans in the secondary market. In the majority of situations, the Bank follows the underwriting guidelines of the various government agencies on residential real estate loans the Bank seeks to portfolio. For the year ended December&#160;31, 2013, the Bank&#8217;s residential real estate loan production was $135.5 million. Of this, sold loans totaled $105.8 million, while portfolio and construction loans totaled $12.3 million and $17.4 million, respectively. Residential real estate net charge-offs in this portfolio in 2013 and 2012 were $2.5 million and $2.2 million respectively. Other residential real estate delinquencies has been moderate, and non-accruals were $4.74 million as of December&#160;31, 2013. The foregoing measures are a reflection of the Bank&#8217;s underwriting and collection practices. The Bank also added full time equivalent resources to its collections department, allowing the Bank to make more frequent and earlier collection calls, resulting in better working relationships with those borrowers who may have difficulty in making timely payments. </FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 24.5pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The economic recession and current recovery has also affected the operations of BKFC and the Bank. During the fourth quarter of 2008 and first quarter of 2009, BKFC and the Bank each participated in two government programs, which had the effect of enabling it to enhance liquidity and to augment its strong capital position and otherwise facilitate its response to the economic crisis. First, in October 2008 the Bank participated in the transaction account guarantee component of the FDIC&#8217;s TLGP program. Second, in February 2009 BKFC participated in the CPP, receiving $34,000,000, in exchange for issuing 34,000 shares of Series A Preferred Stock and a Warrant to purchase approximately 274,784 shares of Common Stock.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;&#160; </FONT>As of December 31, 2013, all of the TARP Series A Preferred Stock has been repurchased by BKFC and in the second quarter of 2013, the Company completed the repurchase of the Warrant.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>As a result of the final repurchase, limitations on increasing dividends, executive compensation and other regulatory requirements are no longer applicable to BKFC.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Neither BKFC nor the Bank actively participates in any of the other federal government programs that have been instituted in response to the current economic recession.</FONT></DIV>

Management&#8217;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations&#8221; in this Annual Report. </FONT></DIV>

  <DIV

<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Lending Activities</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"> </FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></B></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">General</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>As a commercial bank, the Bank offers a wide variety of loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Among the Bank&#8217;s various lending activities are the origination of loans secured by first mortgages on nonresidential real estate; loans secured by first mortgages on one- to four-family residences; unsecured commercial loans and commercial loans secured by various assets of the borrower; unsecured consumer loans and consumer loans secured by automobiles, boats and recreational vehicles; and construction and land development loans secured by mortgages on the underlying property.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>

  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: -0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt 0.5in; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Nonresidential Real Estate Loans</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank makes loans secured by first mortgages on nonresidential real estate, including retail stores, office buildings, warehouses, apartment buildings and recreational facilities.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Such mortgage loans generally have maturities between 5 and 10 years with amortization periods of 10 to 20 years and are made with adjustable interest rates tied to a spread over LIBOR or a comparable U.S. Treasury index (&#8220;ARMs&#8221;).<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Interest rates on LIBOR based loans typically adjust every 30 days, while the ARMs adjust every one-, three- or five-years based upon the interest rates of the applicable one-, three- or five- year U.S. Treasury security then offered.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Bank limits the amount of each loan in relationship, in accordance with the Bank&#8217;s policy, to the appraised value of the real estate and improvements at the time of origination of a nonresidential real estate loan.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In accordance with regulations, the maximum loan-to-value ratio (the &#8220;LTV&#8221;) on nonresidential real estate loans made by the Bank ranges from 65% to 85%, depending on property type.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Nonresidential real estate lending is generally considered to involve a higher degree of risk than residential lending.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Such risk is due primarily to the dependence of the borrower on the cash flow from the property to service the loan.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>If the cash flow from the property is reduced due to a downturn in the economy, for example, or due to any other reason, the borrower&#8217;s ability to repay the loan may be impaired.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>To reduce such risk, the decision to underwrite a nonresidential real estate loan is based primarily on the quality and characteristics of the income stream generated by the property and/or the business of the borrower and any other applicable credit enhancement, such as global cash flow analysis.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In addition, the Bank generally obtains the personal guarantees of one or more of the principals of the borrower and carefully evaluates the location of the real estate, the quality of the management operating the property, the debt service ratio and appraisals supporting the property&#8217;s valuation.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">At December 31, 2013, the Bank had a total of $571 million in nonresidential real estate loans, the vast majority of which were secured by property located in the northern Kentucky and the Greater Cincinnati metropolitan area.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Owner-occupied nonresidential real estate was $302 million of the total nonresidential real estate loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Total nonresidential real estate loans comprised approximately 46% of the Bank&#8217;s total loans at such date, $9.16 million of which were classified as non-performing.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Residential Real Estate Loans</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank originates permanent conventional loans secured by first mortgages on single-family and 1-4 family residential properties located in the northern Kentucky area.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank also originates<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>loans for the construction of residential properties and home equity loans secured by second mortgages on residential real estate.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Each such loans is secured by a mortgage on the underlying real estate and any improvements thereon.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The residential real estate loans originated for the Bank&#8217;s loan portfolio are either one- or three-year ARMs.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Such loans typically have adjustment period caps of 2% and lifetime caps of 6%.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The maximum amortization period of such loans is 30 years.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank does not engage in the practice of deeply discounting the initial rates on such loans, nor does the Bank engage in the practice of putting payment caps on loans that could lead to negative amortization.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Historically, the Bank has not made fixed-rate residential mortgage loans for its portfolio.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In order to meet consumer demand for fixed-rate loans, however, the Bank has originated and sold loans to other lenders willing to accept the interest rate and credit risk.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">

  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">While in a rising interest rate environment the delinquency and foreclosure rates associated with interest rate resets on residential real estate loans could increase, this risk is somewhat mitigated by the 2% period cap and the 6% lifetime cap on the typical loan in the Bank&#8217;s residential real estate portfolio.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Furthermore, the aggregate amount of residential real estate loans held by the Bank does not represent a significant portion of the Bank&#8217;s overall loan portfolio.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Accordingly, the risks associated with a material increase in delinquencies and foreclosures resulting upon the occurrence of any interest rate reset are minimal.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">BKFC does not have higher risk loans such as subprime loans, &#8220;alt A&#8221; loans, no or little documentation loans, interest-only or option adjustable rate mortgage products in its portfolio.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The majority of the Bank&#8217;s residential portfolio would be considered conforming loans in accordance with standards of governmental agencies.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Bank requires private mortgage insurance for the amount of any such loan with an LTV in excess of 90%.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The aggregate amount of the Bank&#8217;s residential real estate loans equaled approximately $283 million at December 31, 2013 and represented 23% of total loans at such date.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>At December 31, 2013, the Bank had $5.36 million of non-performing loans of this type.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Loans Held for Sale</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank originates residential real estate loans to be sold, service released, subject to commitment to purchase in the secondary market.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>These loans are fixed rate with terms ranging from fifteen to thirty years.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>At December 31, 2013, these loans totaled $3.2 million.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Commercial Loans</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank offers commercial loans to individuals and businesses located throughout northern Kentucky and the Greater Cincinnati metropolitan area.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The typical commercial borrower is a small to mid-sized company with annual sales under $20 million.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The majority of commercial loans are made with adjustable rates of interest tied to the Bank&#8217;s prime interest rate.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Commercial loans typically have terms of one to five years.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In general, commercial lending entails significant risks.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Such loans are subject to greater risk of default during periods of adverse economic conditions.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Because such loans are secured by equipment, inventory, accounts receivable and other non-real estate assets, the collateral may not be sufficient to ensure full payment of the loan in the event of a default.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>To reduce such risk, the Bank generally obtains personal guarantees from one or more of the principals backing the borrower.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>At December 31, 2013, the Bank had $242 million, or 19% of total loans, in commercial loans, $385,000 of which were classified as non-performing.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Consumer Loans.</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank makes a variety of consumer loans, including automobile loans, recreational vehicle loans and personal loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Such loans generally have fixed rates with terms from three to five years.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Consumer loans involve a higher risk of default than residential real estate loans, particularly in the case of consumer loans that are unsecured or secured by depreciating assets, such as automobiles.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Repossessed collateral for a defaulted consumer loan may not provide an adequate source of repayment of the outstanding loan balance as a result of the greater likelihood of damage, loss or depreciation, and the remaining deficiency may not warrant further substantial collection efforts against the borrower.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In addition, consumer loan collections depend on the borrower&#8217;s continuing financial stability, and thus are more likely to be adversely affected by job loss, illness or personal bankruptcy.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Various federal and state laws, including federal and state bankruptcy and insolvency laws, may also limit the amount that can be recovered on such loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>At December 31, 2013, the Bank had $16 million, or 1% of total loans, in consumer loans, $27,000 of which were classified as non-performing.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Construction and Land Development Loans</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank makes loans for the construction of residential and nonresidential real estate and land development purposes.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Most of these loans are structured with adjustable rates of interest tied to changes in the Bank&#8217;s prime interest rate for the period of construction.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>A general contractor is used with the majority of the construction loans originated by the Bank to owner-occupants for the construction of single-family homes.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Other loans are made to builders and developers for various projects, including the construction of homes and other buildings that may have not been pre-sold or to finance the preparation of land for site and project development.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Construction and land development loans involve greater underwriting and default risks than do loans secured by mortgages on improved and developed properties, due to the effects of general economic conditions on real estate developments, developers, managers and builders.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In addition, such loans are more challenging to evaluate and monitor.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Loan funds are advanced upon the security of the project under construction, which is more challenging to value before the completion of construction.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Moreover, because of the uncertainties inherent in estimating construction costs, it is challenging to evaluate accurately the value upon completion and the total loan funds required to complete a project.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In the event a default on a construction or land development loan, it may be necessary for the Bank to take control of the project and attempt either to arrange for completion of construction or dispose of the unfinished project.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>At December 31, 2013, a total of $103 million, or approximately 8% of the Bank&#8217;s total loans, consisted of construction and land development loans, $510,000 of which were classified as non-performing.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>
<B>  <TABLE
style="WIDTH: 100%">
    <TR>  <TD
style="WIDTH: 33%; VERTICAL-ALIGN: bottom" align="left">
</TD>
  <TD
style="FONT-STYLE: normal; WIDTH: 34%; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; VERTICAL-ALIGN: bottom; FONT-WEIGHT: normal" align="center">
8</TD>
  <TD
style="WIDTH: 33%; VERTICAL-ALIGN: bottom" align="right">
</TD>
</TR>
  <TR>  <TD><BR /></TD>
</TR>
</TABLE>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;BACKGROUND-COLOR: rgb(0,0,0); FONT-STYLE: normal; PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always; TEXT-INDENT: 0in; MARGIN: 0in; HEIGHT: 1px; CLEAR: both; FONT-SIZE: 1px" contenteditable="false">
</DIV>
</B>  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Municipal Obligations</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank makes loans to various Kentucky municipalities for various purposes, including the construction of municipal buildings and equipment purchases.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Loans made to municipalities are usually secured by mortgages on the properties or financed by a lien on equipment purchased or by the general taxing authority of the municipality and provide certain tax benefits for the Bank.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>At December 31, 2013, the Bank had $36 million, or 3% of total loans, invested in municipal obligation loans, none of which were classified as non-performing. </FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Loan Solicitation and Processing</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank&#8217;s loan originations are developed from a number of sources, including its existing customer base, periodic newspaper and radio advertisements, solicitations by the Bank&#8217;s lending staff, walk-in customers, director referrals and an officer call program.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>For nonresidential real estate loans, the Bank obtains information with respect to the credit, business and financial history of the borrower and its current and prior real estate projects.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Personal guarantees of one or more principals of the borrower are generally obtained.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>For loans that meet or exceed a certain dollar threshold, an environmental study of such real estate is normally conducted.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Upon the completion of the appraisal of the nonresidential real estate and the receipt of information on the borrower, the loan package is submitted to the Bank&#8217;s Loan Committee if the amount and/or relationship exceed the officer&#8217;s lending authority for approval or rejection.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>If, however, the loan relationship is in excess of $2.50 million, the loan will be submitted to the Bank&#8217;s Executive Loan Committee for approval or rejection.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">In connection with residential real estate loans, the Bank obtains a credit report, verification of employment and other documentation concerning the creditworthiness of the borrower.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>An appraisal of the fair market value of the real estate on which the Bank will be granted a mortgage to secure the loan is prepared by an independent fee appraiser approved by the Bank&#8217;s Board of Directors.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>An environmental study of such real estate is conducted only if the appraiser or Bank has reason to believe that an environmental problem may exist.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">When a residential real estate loan application is approved, title insurance is normally obtained in respect of the real estate, which will secure the loan.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>At the time a nonresidential real estate loan is closed, title insurance is customarily obtained on the title to the real estate, which will secure the mortgage loan.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>All borrowers are required to carry satisfactory fire and casualty insurance and flood insurance, if applicable, and name the Bank as an insured mortgagee.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Commercial loans are underwritten primarily on the basis of the stability of the income and cash flows generated by the business and/or property.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>For most commercial loans, however, the personal guarantees of one or more principals of the borrowers are generally obtained.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Consumer loans are underwritten on the basis of the borrower&#8217;s credit history and an analysis of the borrower&#8217;s income and expenses, ability to repay the loan and the value of any collateral.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The procedure for approval of construction loans is the same as for permanent mortgage loans, except that an appraiser evaluates the building plans, construction specifications and estimates of construction costs.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank also evaluates the feasibility of the proposed construction project and the experience and record of the builder.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 30.25pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Loan Origination and Other Fees.</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank realizes loan origination fees and other fee income from its lending activities and also realizes income from late payment charges, application fees and fees for other miscellaneous services.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Loan origination fees and other fees are a volatile source of income, varying with the volume of lending, loan repayments and general economic conditions.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Nonrefundable loan origination fees and certain direct loan origination costs are deferred and recognized as an adjustment to yield over the life of the related loan. </FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 30.25pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Delinquent Loans, Non-Performing Assets, Classified Assets and Troubled Debt Restructurings (TDRs).</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>When a borrower fails to make a required payment on a loan, the Bank attempts to cause the deficiency to be cured by contacting the borrower.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In most cases, deficiencies are cured promptly as a result of these collection efforts.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Loans that are 90 days past due or more that are not considered well secured and in the process of collection are placed on non-accrual status.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Under-collateralized loans that are 90 days past due or more in which the Bank does not expect to be repaid by the borrower&#8217;s or guarantor&#8217;s financial wherewithal after an extensive collection effort, shall be reviewed for full or partial charge-off.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The amount charged-off will be charged against the allowance for loan losses.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Bank utilizes a risk-rating system to quantify and monitor loan quality.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The system assigns a risk rating from one to nine for each loan.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Classified commercial loans are those with risk ratings of seven or higher.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Each loan rating is determined by analyzing the borrowers&#8217; management, financial ability, sales trends, operating results, financial conditions, asset protection, contingencies, payment history, financial flexibility, credit enhancements and other relevant factors.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Loans that fall into the classified categories are monitored on a regular basis and proper action is taken to minimize the Bank&#8217;s loss exposure.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Losses or partial losses are recognized when loans are deemed uncollectible.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>

  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 30.25pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Bank&#8217;s risk rating system was developed in a manner that is consistent with the regulatory guidance.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Problem assets are classified as &#8220;special mention&#8221; (risk rating 6), &#8220;substandard&#8221; (risk rating 7), &#8220;substandard non-accrual&#8221; (risk rating 8), or &#8220;doubtful&#8221; (risk rating 9).<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>&#8220;Substandard&#8221; assets have one or more defined weaknesses and are characterized by the distinct possibility that the insured institution will sustain some loss if the deficiencies are not corrected.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>&#8220;Doubtful&#8221; assets have the same weaknesses as &#8220;substandard&#8221; assets, with the additional characteristics that (i) the weaknesses make collection or liquidation in full on the basis of currently existing facts, conditions and values questionable and (ii) there is a high possibility of loss.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The regulations also contain a &#8220;special mention&#8221; or also known as &#8220;criticized assets&#8221; category, consisting of assets which do not currently expose an institution to a sufficient degree of risk to warrant classification but which possess credit deficiencies or potential weaknesses deserving management&#8217;s close attention.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The following table sets forth information with respect to the Bank&#8217;s non-performing assets for the periods indicated.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In addition, the Bank evaluates loans to identify those that are &#8220;impaired.&#8221;<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Impaired loans are those for which management has determined that it is probable that the customer will be unable to comply with the contractual terms of the loan.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Loans so identified are reduced (i) to the fair value of the collateral securing the loan, (ii) to the present value of expected future cash flows, or (iii) to the market price of the loan based upon readily available information for that type of loan, by the allocation of a portion of the allowance for loan losses to the loan.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>As of December 31, 2013, the Bank had designated $29 million as impaired loans, and a portion of these loans were included in the non-accrual and 90 days past due and troubled debt restructurings totals below. Management evaluates for impairment all loans selected for specific review during its quarterly allowance for loan losses analysis.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Generally, the impairment analysis does not address smaller balance consumer credits.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The credit quality table detailing loans by grade, the non-performing loan table and the aging of past due table include measurements which management believes are the best indicators of potential problem loans and there were no other known potential problem loans beyond what is disclosed in these tables at December 31, 2013.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></B></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Allowance for Loan Losses</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>While management believes that it uses the best information available to determine the allowance for loan losses, unforeseen market conditions could result in adjustments, and net earnings could be significantly affected if circumstances differ substantially from the assumptions used in making the final determination.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>At December 31, 2013, the Bank&#8217;s allowance for loan losses totaled $16.3 million.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">On at least a quarterly basis, a formal analysis of the adequacy of the allowance is prepared and reviewed by senior management and the Bank&#8217;s Board of Directors.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>This analysis serves as a point in time assessment of the level of the allowance and serves as a basis for provisions for loan losses.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The loan quality monitoring process includes assigning loan grades and the use of a watch list to identify loans of concern.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The analysis of the allowance for loan losses includes the allocation of specific amounts of the allowance to individual problem loans, generally based on an analysis of the collateral securing those loans.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Portions of the allowance are also allocated to loans based on their risk rating with the higher the risk rating, the higher the allowance allocated to that loan.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>These components are added together and compared to the balance of our allowance at the evaluation date. </FONT></DIV>

  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Deposits and Borrowings</FONT></B></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">General.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Deposits have traditionally been the primary source of the Bank&#8217;s funds for use in lending and other investment activities.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>In addition to deposits, the Bank derives funds from interest payments and principal repayments on loans and income on earning assets.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Loan payments are a relatively stable source of funds, while deposit inflows and outflows fluctuate more in response to economic conditions and interest rates.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank has lines of credit established at its major correspondent banks to purchase federal funds to meet liquidity needs.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank may also borrow funds from the FHLB in the form of advances.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Bank also uses retail repurchase agreements as a source of funds.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>These agreements essentially represent borrowings by the Bank from customers with maturities of three months or less.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Certain securities are pledged as collateral for these agreements.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>At December 31, 2013, the Bank had $27.6 million in retail repurchase agreements.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Bank also entered into a capital lease obligation for a branch in 1997 with a term of 20 years and a monthly payment of $4,000.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Deposits.</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Deposits are attracted principally from within the Bank&#8217;s designated lending area through the offering of numerous deposit instruments, including regular passbook savings accounts, negotiable order of withdrawal (&#8220;NOW&#8221;) accounts, money market deposit accounts, term certificate accounts and individual retirement accounts (&#8220;IRAs&#8221;).<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Interest rates paid, maturity terms, service fees and withdrawal penalties for the various types of accounts are established periodically by the Bank&#8217;s Board of Directors based on the Bank&#8217;s liquidity requirements, growth goals and market trends.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank may on occasion use brokers to attract deposits.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank did not have brokered deposits as of December 31, 2013.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>

style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 30.25pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">

  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 30.25pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B></B>&#160;</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.4in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Long-Term Borrowings</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">. Long-term consist of $5 million in advances from the Federal Home Loan Bank, $18.6 in trust preferred securities, $20 million in subordinate debentures issued by&#160;US Bank and a $1.9 note payable from US Bank. Further details of these borrowings can be found in note 8 of the accompanying financial statements.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 30.25pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B></B>&#160;</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 30.25pt; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Asset/Liability Management.</FONT></B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank&#8217;s earnings depend primarily upon its net interest income, which is the difference between its interest income on its interest-earning assets, such as mortgage loans and investment securities, and its interest expense paid on its interest-bearing liabilities, consisting of deposits and borrowings.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>As market interest rates change, asset yields and liability costs do not change simultaneously.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Due to maturity, re-pricing and timing differences of interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities, earnings will be affected differently under various interest rate scenarios.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank has sought to limit these net income fluctuations and manage interest rate risk by originating adjustable-rate loans and purchasing relatively short-term and variable-rate investments and securities.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>
  <TABLE
style="WIDTH: 100%">
    <TR>  <TD
style="WIDTH: 33%; VERTICAL-ALIGN: bottom" align="left">
</TD>
  <TD
style="FONT-STYLE: normal; WIDTH: 34%; FONT-FAMILY: Times New Roman; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; VERTICAL-ALIGN: bottom; FONT-WEIGHT: normal" align="center">
14</TD>
  <TD
style="WIDTH: 33%; VERTICAL-ALIGN: bottom" align="right">
</TD>
</TR>
  <TR>  <TD><BR /></TD>
</TR>
</TABLE>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;BACKGROUND-COLOR: rgb(0,0,0); FONT-STYLE: normal; PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always; TEXT-INDENT: 0in; MARGIN: 0in; HEIGHT: 1px; CLEAR: both; FONT-SIZE: 1px" contenteditable="false">
</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;CLEAR: both">
&#160;</DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Bank&#8217;s interest rate spread is the principal determinant of the Bank&#8217;s net interest income.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The interest rate spread can vary considerably over time because asset and liability re-pricing do not coincide.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Moreover, the long-term and cumulative effect of interest rate changes can be substantial.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Interest rate risk is defined as the sensitivity of an institution&#8217;s earnings and net asset values to changes in interest rates.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The ability to maximize net interest income is largely dependent upon sustaining a positive interest rate spread during fluctuations in the prevailing level of interest rates.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Interest rate sensitivity is a measure of the difference between amounts of interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities, which either re-price or mature within a given period of time. The difference, or the interest rate re-pricing &#8220;gap,&#8221; provides an indication of the extent to which a financial institution&#8217;s interest rate spread will be affected by changes in interest rates.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>A positive gap occurs when interest-earning assets exceed interest-bearing liabilities re-pricing during a designated time frame.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Conversely, a negative gap occurs when interest-bearing liabilities exceed interest-earning assets re-pricing within a designated time frame.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Generally, during a period of rising interest rates, a negative gap would adversely affect net interest income, while a positive gap would result in an increase in net interest income, and during a period of falling interest rates, a negative gap would result in an increase in net interest income, while a positive gap would have the opposite effect.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">In recognition of the foregoing factors, the management and the Board of Directors of the Bank have implemented an asset and liability management strategy directed toward maintaining a reasonable degree of interest rate sensitivity.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The principal elements of such strategy include: (i) meeting the consumer preference for fixed-rate loans by establishing a correspondent lending program that has enabled the Bank to originate and sell fixed-rate mortgage loans; (ii)&#160;maintaining relatively short weighted-average terms to maturity in the securities portfolio as a hedge against rising interest rates; (iii) emphasizing the origination and retention of adjustable-rate loans; and (iv) utilizing longer term certificates of deposit as funding sources when available.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Management and the Board of Directors monitor the Bank&#8217;s exposure to interest rate risk on a monthly basis to ensure the interest rate risk is maintained within an acceptable range.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>For more information on the Bank&#8217;s interest rate risk see the &#8220;Asset/Liability Management and Market Risk&#8221; section of &#8220;Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosure about Market Risk&#8221;. </FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The following table sets forth the amounts of the Bank&#8217;s interest-earning assets and interest-bearing liabilities outstanding at December 31, 2013, which are scheduled to re-price or mature in each of the time periods shown.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The amounts of assets and liabilities shown which re-price or mature in a given period were determined in accordance with the contractual terms of the asset or liability.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The table shows that the maturity or re-pricing of the Bank&#8217;s liabilities exceed the contractual terms to maturity or re-pricing of the Bank&#8217;s earning assets in a twelve-month period by $266 million.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT></FONT></DIV>

  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<B><FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Competition</FONT></B></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">There is significant competition within the banking and financial services industry in northern Kentucky, which is the primary market in which the Bank operates.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Changes in regulation, technology and product delivery systems have resulted in an increasingly competitive environment.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank expects to continue to face increasing competition from online and traditional financial institutions seeking to attract customers by providing access to similar services and products.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Some of the institutions which compete with the Bank are among the largest financial institutions in the United States.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Any actual intervention or assistance to these competitors made by the U.S. federal government, as well as the perception that such assistance would be forthcoming if needed, could have the effect of eroding any competitive advantages of the Bank in the markets in which it operates.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Within the northern Kentucky and greater Cincinnati, Ohio markets, the Bank competes with approximately six financial institutions with over $50 billion in total assets, as well as numerous state chartered banking institutions of comparable or larger size and resources and smaller community banking organizations.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank also has numerous local, regional and national nonbank competitors, including savings and loan associations, credit unions, mortgage companies, insurance companies, finance companies, financial service operations of major retailers, investment brokerage and financial advisory firms and mutual fund companies.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Because nonbank financial institutions are not subject to the same regulatory restrictions as banks and bank holding companies, they can often operate with greater flexibility and lower cost structures.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Currently, the Bank does not face meaningful competition from international banks in its market, although that could change in the future.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Bank competes for deposits primarily with other commercial banks, savings associations and credit unions and with the issuers of commercial paper and other securities, such as shares in money market mutual funds. The primary factors in competing for deposits are interest rates and convenience of office locations.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The Bank competes for making loans primarily with other banks, savings associations, consumer finance companies, credit unions, leasing companies and other nonbank competitors. The Bank competes for loan originations primarily through the interest rates and loan fees it charges and through the efficiency and quality of services it provides to borrowers. Competition for loans is affected by, among other things, the general availability of lendable funds, general and local economic conditions, current interest rate levels and other factors that are not readily predictable.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;TEXT-INDENT: 0.5in; MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Due to the Bank&#8217;s size relative to the many other financial institutions in its market, management believes that the Bank does not have a substantial share of the deposit and loan markets. The table below presents FDIC deposit data regarding the Bank&#8217;s deposit market share.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>The June 2013 data set forth below are the most current data available from the FDIC at this time and represents those counties in which the Bank has reported market share for deposits.</FONT></DIV>
  <DIV
style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">
<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</FONT></DIV>

style="CLEAR:both;MARGIN: 0in 0in 0pt; CLEAR: both" align="justify">

<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Services provided by the Bank&#8217;s trust division face competition from many national, regional and local financial institutions.<FONT style="FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160; </FONT>Companies that offer broad services similar to those provided by the Bank, such as other banks, trust companies and full service brokerage firms, as well as companies that specialize in particular services offered by the Bank, such as investment advisors and mutual fund providers, all compete with the Bank&#8217;s trust division.</FONT></DIV>
